beats.text: The memory architecture is divided into User Space and Kernel Space.
In User Space, execution begins at the Database Process.
The process initiates an asynchronous write call.
This is followed by a synchronous fsync operation.
The write call routes into the Page Cache within Kernel Space and returns immediately, creating dirty pages.
The Kernel Flusher Thread periodically handles writebacks from the Page Cache.
Requests pass into the I/O Queue, while fsync waits for disk completion.
At the bottom is Persistent Storage, containing the Block Device.
Finally, enqueued operations are flushed from the I/O Queue down to the Block Device.
The diagram introduces key architectural conventions, including average aggregation, depthwise convolutions, and trainable scaling parameters.
In the Swin-Transformer block, input features pass through layer normalization alongside an initial residual shortcut.
Normalized features enter the window and shifted-window multi-head self-attention module to capture spatial context.
The attention outputs are then merged with the initial residual connection.
The first Mona adapter layer processes the aggregated representation to enhance visual feature adaptation.
Features undergo a second layer normalization step before the feed-forward network, accompanied by another skip connection.
A feed-forward layer then transforms the intermediate token representations.
The feed-forward output is summed with its corresponding shortcut.
A second Mona layer further refines the features before outputting the final representation of the Swin-Transformer block.
Inside the Mona layer, input features undergo layer normalization scaled by a trainable factor, while a parallel skip branch is scaled by a second factor.
The scaled feature streams are combined at an addition node to regulate input distribution.
A down projection layer reduces channel dimensionality before branching into multi-scale convolutional paths and residual shortcuts.
Three parallel depthwise convolutions with 3x3, 5x5, and 7x7 kernels extract multi-scale visual patterns.
Outputs from all three kernel branches are combined using an averaging operation.
The averaged depthwise feature is added to the pre-convolution residual branch.
A 1x1 convolution aggregates point-wise channel features alongside an adjacent residual shortcut.
The 1x1 convolution output is summed with its shortcut connection.
A GeLU activation function introduces non-linearity.
An up projection layer restores the original feature channel dimensions.
Finally, the outer residual is added to yield the complete output of the Mona layer.
The pipeline begins in Section A with Hierarchical Blocks, taking an initial descriptive text prompt for analysis.
The prompt is analyzed to determine the optimization order based on occlusion hierarchy.
Block one targets more occluded items first, beginning with a coarse base human avatar.
It then performs precise optimization on the yellow shirt.
Next, optimization proceeds to the pink trousers, linking into the detailed part-optimization workflow.
Finally, the blue leather shoes are refined to complete Block one.
In Section B, Part-Segmentation isolates the trousers using two-dimensional segment probabilities.
The segmented part is isolated and passed to fine-grained optimization guided by the text prompt.
SDS loss is applied to produce the avatar with precisely rendered pink trousers.
The automatic pipeline extends across sequential blocks toward less occluded layers.
In Block n b, the outermost black coat is added coarsely and then refined to a precise state.
Section C outlines Gaussian Extension, where new Gaussian kernels are densified for adding a coat.
The densified avatar is optimized using SDS loss and passed into Label Elimination to remove redundant kernels.
This results in a clean avatar model with the extended garment layer.
Section D breaks down Label Elimination, starting from original Gaussian kernels and densifying new ones.
SAM is applied to segment part semantics and assign labels to the Gaussian kernels.
Redundant newly added kernels that do not belong to the new part are eliminated.
Only the original and segment Gaussian kernels are retained in the final structure.
To begin, input egocentric video frames are fed into a frozen video transformer backbone.
The visual encoder extracts spatio-temporal feature maps representing the video sequence.
In parallel, narration sentences and extracted noun phrases pass through a frozen text backbone.
This yields a global sentence embedding along with fine-grained noun embeddings.
A set of learnable queries is defined, consisting of hand queries, object queries, and a global video query.
The object-aware decoder uses cross-attention to allow these queries to attend to the visual feature map.
The decoder produces localized summary vectors for hands and objects, as well as a video-level embedding.
During training, auxiliary box and semantic heads predict spatial bounding boxes and semantic object classes from the summary vectors.
Finally, the model is trained jointly with bounding box loss, cross-modal video-text contrastive loss, and word-level grounding loss.
The framework begins with an input portrait image.
A geometry-aware encoder projects the input image into the latent space.
This yields an extended latent code representing coarse geometry and appearance.
The latent code is passed into a pre-trained generator, extracting intermediate feature maps while building a 3D tri-plane representation.
The resulting tri-plane encapsulates the canonical 3D volume synthesized from the latent code.
A neural rendering decoder then renders the volume under the estimated camera pose.
This produces an initial coarse reconstruction of the input face.
Next, the framework computes an image residual between the input and its initial reconstruction, pairing it with the generator feature maps.
The Adaptive Feature Alignment module aligns these residual features into the canonical space using cross-attention.
This produces refined latent feature maps containing restored fine-grained textural details.
These modified features are then forwarded through the remaining generator layers.
This constructs a refined tri-plane while identifying visible and occluded 3D point sets based on the input view.
An occlusion-aware fusion combines the visible refined details with the base tri-plane to prevent distortion in unobserved regions.
The mixed tri-plane is then supplied to the neural rendering decoder under the target camera pose.
Finally, the system renders the high-fidelity inversion image with precise identity details and 3D consistency.
The pipeline begins with the editing guidance generation stage to convert user edits into supervision signals.
A pretrained teacher model encapsulates the original neural radiance field of the reconstructed scene.
When a user interactively edits a region, such as scaling an object, a spatial mapping function is established.
Sampled points and ray directions in the edited target space are mapped back to the source space, querying the teacher model to obtain color and density guidance.
This generated guidance is then transferred to a two-stage student training framework designed for instant preview.
Student supervision combines a local loss on the edited object with a global loss over the entire scene.
During local pretraining, only local feature parameters are updated while decoder weights remain frozen, enabling instant preview within one second.
In the second stage, global fine-tuning refines the entire scene network using full supervision from teacher inference.
The resulting student model delivers fully converged, high-fidelity rendering of the edited 3D scene.
The pipeline begins by taking the input image alongside a spatially augmented positive sample.
A set of negative image samples capturing varied crowd scenes and weather conditions is also gathered.
All image samples are passed into a shared VGG encoder.
The encoder extracts deep image feature representations for the positive, input, and negative samples.
Within the Contrastive Weather-adaptive Module, these features are fed into a weather encoder.
The weather encoder outputs corresponding weight vectors for each branch.
A weather bank maintains learned weather prototypes, regularized by a compact prototype loss.
The weight vectors and the weather bank are combined through matrix multiplication.
This multiplication yields patch-wise weather-adaptive queries across the positive, input, and negative branches.
A contrastive loss optimizes the queries, while the input weather query is forwarded through a multi-layer perceptron.
In the weather-aware crowd counting stage, a transformer decoder takes the weather query along with keys and values from the input features.
The transformer decoder produces weather-aware crowd counting features.
A final decoder processes these crowd counting features.
Finally, the model generates the predicted crowd density map, trained under a Bayesian loss.
The training pipeline begins with the Breast Cancer Image Dataset, providing source data for segmentation and classification workflows.
In the segmentation branch, raw ultrasonography images are extracted from the dataset.
These images enter the preprocessing stage,
where they undergo dimension scaling to 128 by 128 pixels followed by pixel normalization.
Simple Linear Iterative Clustering (SLIC) then clusters pixels into superpixels to mitigate noise.
The clustered images are fed into a modified U-Net encoder-decoder network alongside ground truth masks.
Completing this training yields the trained segmentation model.
In parallel, masked images and corresponding class labels are retrieved for detection training.
A pre-trained VGG 16 model extracts deep spatial features from these masked ultrasound images.
Extracted features are processed through five fully connected dense layers with dropout and activations.
This establishes the trained detection model for classifying tumor types.
Finally, the trained components combine into the unified breast cancer detection pipelining framework.
The pipeline begins with a sequence of five hundred twelve dimensional input feature vectors.
These vectors are organized into an input feature matrix labeled F sub w, with dimensions five hundred twelve by n.
Inside the scaled dot product attention sub-block, the matrix branches through fully connected layers into key transpose, query, and value matrices.
The key transpose and query representations are multiplied together and processed by a softmax function.
This yields an n-by-n matrix of self-attention weights labeled W sub s a.
The self-attention weights are then multiplied with the value matrix.
The result feeds into the cross-walk attention sub-block as an intermediate matrix labeled H sub a.
A per-row softmax operation is then applied across the matrix columns.
Next, the softmax output is combined element-wise with a bypass connection from the original matrix F sub w.
This creates the cross-walk attention matrix labeled G, with dimensions five hundred twelve by n.
The column vectors are then aggregated through a summation operation.
Finally, the system outputs the five hundred twelve dimensional feature vector labeled f sub a.
The legend outlines the core modules, including SSFT, SFT, residual blocks, and convolutional layers.
The pipeline begins with a blurred face image as input.
Within the deblurring stream, the input image enters the encoder through an initial convolution layer labeled E zero.
The first encoder stage processes feature maps through residual blocks followed by a downsampling convolution.
A second stage further extracts features and downsamples the spatial resolution.
The encoder concludes at bottleneck stage E four to form compact feature representations.
Features from each intermediate encoder stage branch into the prior estimation stream via SSFT modules and residual blocks.
This stream outputs multi-scale estimated priors labeled P-hat one, P-hat two, and P-hat three.
In the decoder, stage D three modulates bottleneck features with estimated prior P-hat three using an SFT module.
Decoder stage D two incorporates estimated prior P-hat two and continues upsampling.
Stage D one modulates with prior P-hat one, combining the decoded features with a skip connection from E zero.
A final convolution block labeled D zero maps the merged representations.
This generates the predicted deblurred image, presented alongside the target ground truth image.
A fixed VGG Face model extracts multi-scale feature priors labeled P one, P two, and P three from the target image.
Prior loss supervises the estimated priors against target features, while pixel loss compares the predicted image to the ground truth.
Finally, a discriminator evaluates sets of estimated and real feature priors to compute the adversarial loss.
The architecture is organized into local and global attention pathways across channel and spatial attention stages, culminating in a fusion module.
The input feature tensor enters the network and branches into both the local and global processing pathways.
In the channel attention stage, both local and global channel attention maps are computed.
The local channel attention map scales the feature stream followed by a residual addition, producing the local channel feature tensor.
Simultaneously, the global channel attention map modulates the input stream to produce the global channel feature tensor.
Next, in the spatial attention stage, separate local and global spatial attention maps are derived.
The local spatial attention map is applied with a residual connection, generating the refined local feature tensor.
Concurrently, the global spatial attention map is applied with a residual addition to output the refined global feature tensor.
In the fusion module, the local features, direct bypass features, and global features are weighted by distinct parameters and summed together.
This produces the final fused output tensor, combining both local and global contextual information.
The pipeline takes K-shot support images and a query image as inputs, referencing the aggregation, tensor shape, and path notations shown in the legend.
Both the support and query images are fed into parallel Backbone Networks for feature extraction.
In the support stream, RoI pooling is performed using the support image ground truth boxes to extract pooled feature tensors.
The query features then combine with the support branch at an aggregation operation labeled Q S A.
The aggregated output flows into the R P N, followed by RoI pooling on the query feature stream.
These pooled query representations merge with the upper support features at the aggregation module labeled Q R A.
Finally, the combined features pass into the RoI Head, generating the final detection bounding boxes on the query image.
The pipeline begins with step one, the robust initializer, which takes an image, a point cloud, or both as an instance-specific prior.
These inputs are passed directly into the Encoder network to produce an intermediate feature representation.
In step two, the Decoder applies a category-specific prior to estimate the signed distance function and decode it into a three-dimensional shape.
The decoded shape is compared against the input point cloud using the data energy term to guide alignment.
In step three, the pipeline optimizes the code by routing the shape into the Discriminator alongside a high-dimensional prior.
The discriminator loss backpropagates through the network, iteratively repeating steps two and three to refine the reconstruction.
[No narration]
The framework begins with multi-view input images capturing the scene from multiple camera perspectives.
A dilated ResNet-18 backbone processes each camera view to extract downsampled two-dimensional feature representations.
A foreground selector module isolates meaningful semantic information, highlighting critical foreground regions.
Through non-parametric three-dimensional feature pulling, projection and bilinear sampling map two-dimensional features into view-specific three-dimensional volumes.
These view-specific feature volumes are then fed into the maximal fusion module.
Max pooling aggregates features across all views, which are concatenated with coordinate volumes and convolved to produce an aggregated three-dimensional feature volume.
Reducing the vertical dimension forms a coarse bird's-eye-view feature map, which is then refined by the large kernel refiner.
The enhanced bird's-eye-view feature representation is subsequently passed through a final convolution layer.
The network outputs the final predicted two-dimensional pedestrian occupancy map.
Finally, the predicted occupancy map is compared against the ground truth using a mean squared error loss.
The pipeline begins with video sequences sampled from the source and target domains over time.
Both video streams undergo background augmentation to mitigate background bias.
A shared feature extractor extracts spatio-temporal representations from the augmented videos.
The extracted features branch into temporal ordering learning, an action classifier, and a gradient reversal layer.
The global-local view aligner and task branches compute the temporal ordering, classification, and alignment losses.
In the view alignment module, features are paired into global-global, cross-scale, and local-local sets.
Dedicated domain classifiers process each global, cross-scale, and local pair separately.
Each classifier outputs an adversarial loss to align temporal representations across multiple granularities.
The framework begins by processing an input video sequence.
A convolutional encoder extracts visual features from each frame in the sequence.
A convolutional G-R-U aggregates temporal context across frames to generate spatio-temporal representations.
These representations are passed to a Slot Attention module to jointly discover objects and model the background.
The module produces a dedicated background slot alongside multiple object slots.
Each slot is associated with a spatial attention map, isolating the background and individual object segments.
The slot representations are weighted by their corresponding attention maps and summed.
A decoder then reconstructs the combined representation back into the video sequence.
The reconstructed sequence is optimized against the input sequence using a mean squared error loss.
Separated motion segments supervise individual object attention maps using a weighted binary cross-entropy loss.
The individual motion segments are aggregated into a combined moving foreground mask.
Finally, the complement of the background mask yields the true foreground, regularized against the motion mask using a negative log likelihood loss.
The architecture begins by taking a sequence of two-dimensional human poses spanning frames one through T as input.
A fully connected layer linearly projects the joints into feature tokens, which are then enriched with spatial position embeddings.
Inside the AGFormer block, features branch into parallel Spatial GCNFormer and Spatial Transformer streams to capture local and global joint relations.
After feature reshaping, representations pass into Temporal GCNFormer and Temporal Transformer modules to model cross-frame temporal dynamics.
The GCNFormer and Transformer feature streams are merged via adaptive fusion across N stacked AGFormer blocks.
The fused representations proceed through an upper fully connected layer to the regression head.
The regression head outputs the final estimated three-dimensional skeletal poses across all time frames.
Panel B details the Spatial MetaFormer, treating individual body joints from one to J as distinct input tokens.
The joint tokens pass through layer normalization and a spatial token mixer, combined with a residual skip connection.
Features then undergo a second layer normalization, channel multilayer perceptron processing, and residual addition.
Panel C outlines the Temporal MetaFormer, where entire pose frames across time steps one through T serve as tokens.
Frame tokens undergo layer normalization, temporal token mixing, and residual addition to model temporal context.
Finally, the temporal representations pass through layer normalization and a channel multilayer perceptron with a residual connection.
The architecture builds upon a pre-trained, frozen CLIP model containing text and image encoders.
In standard CLIP, the text encoder processes natural language prompts such as 'photo of a cat'.
In parallel, the image encoder extracts visual features from corresponding images.
A contrastive loss trains both encoders to align text and image representations within a shared embedding space.
To train LidarCLIP, automotive camera frames are passed through the frozen CLIP image encoder without gradient updates.
Synchronized point clouds from image-lidar pairs are concurrently processed by a trainable lidar encoder.
A similarity loss maximizes the alignment between lidar and image embeddings, effectively connecting point clouds to text via the image domain.
For text-to-lidar retrieval, a natural language query is mapped into feature space using the frozen text encoder.
Candidate point cloud scans are embedded through the trained lidar encoder.
Optionally, camera images can also be encoded to support multi-modal retrieval under challenging scenarios.
A similarity ranking module then identifies and retrieves the point cloud matching the query.
At inference, the trained lidar encoder embeds point cloud inputs into the unified feature space for downstream tasks.
For lidar-to-image generation, the lidar embedding directly conditions a diffusion model to synthesize realistic visual scenes.
For lidar-to-text generation, the embedding feeds into a captioning model to produce descriptive text of the driving scene.
For zero-shot classification, candidate category labels inserted into text prompt templates are encoded into text embeddings.
Measuring the similarity between the lidar embedding and text embeddings yields zero-shot classification scores across target categories.
The TAG-HGT framework begins by receiving cold-start nodes represented solely by raw text.
These raw textual inputs are passed into the Semantic Feature Encoder.
Within this encoder, a frozen large language model processes the text to extract rich semantic features offline.
Concurrently, warm topology from the existing academic graph is fed into the Temporal Topology Encoder.
A trainable Heterogeneous Graph Transformer encodes these relational graph connections into structural embeddings.
Both the semantic features and structural embeddings are forwarded to the contrastive learning module.
The Cross-View Contrastive Learning module aligns the semantic teacher view with the graph student view via contrastive loss.
The aligned student embeddings and temporal candidate indices enter the Time-Aware Retrieval inference stage.
Candidate retrieval is performed using fast approximate nearest neighbor search followed by time decay filtering.
Finally, the framework delivers high-precision Top-K recommendations in real time.
First, the framework initiates the uncertainty-aware initial human motion estimation module to predict preliminary full-body motion along with joint uncertainty.
Sparse tracking signals from the head and hand controllers are embedded into observation feature representations.
Concurrently, historical human motion sequences are processed through a pose encoder to extract motion history embeddings.
The observation and historical motion representations are concatenated into a shallow motion representation and combined with temporal position embeddings.
A transformer encoder then models temporal dependencies across frames, extracting high-dimensional motion features.
These features feed into a pose regression head to estimate initial poses, while an uncertainty estimation head quantifies joint-level uncertainty.
In the environment point cloud embedding module, the 3D scene point cloud is cropped locally around the estimated human trajectory.
The cropped points are sampled and encoded by a scene encoder to yield environment scene features.
In the refinement stage, uncertainty-guided sampling generates motion hypotheses, while relative head height is computed against the local terrain.
The sampled poses, head translation, and extended observations are concatenated to form unified motion embeddings.
A motion-environment cross-attention module integrates environmental semantics with the motion tokens to produce refined motion representations.
Finally, contact probabilities are estimated and combined with the refined representation to regress the physically plausible final full-body motion.
During the blind time between active sensor frames where LiDAR and image data are unavailable, an asynchronous event camera captures continuous spatiotemporal measurements.
These continuous event streams are converted into voxel grids and encoded into two-dimensional event feature representations.
At the initial active timestamp, synchronized camera images and LiDAR point clouds are collected by the region proposal network.
The network extracts two-dimensional image features and constructs three-dimensional voxel feature grids.
Combining these multi-modal features generates initial three-dimensional bounding box proposals for the active timestamp.
In the Virtual 3D Event Fusion module, event features are projected into virtual 3D space and aligned with the initial bounding boxes and shared voxel features.
Region of interest pooling is applied separately to virtual event and voxel features within each proposal to form fused region features.
During blind time motion prediction, an implicit motion field is generated to estimate explicit motion vectors and a motion confidence score for each object.
Simultaneously, parallel proposal tracks derive their respective implicit motion fields and confidence metrics.
Finally, the predicted spatial shifts and rotations update the bounding boxes, producing accurate 3D object detections at arbitrary inter-frame timestamps.
Existing reconstruction-based detection methods split the pipeline into two disconnected stages.
In the first stage, an input image is passed through a pre-trained diffusion model to produce a reconstructed image.
A conceptual barrier isolates the two stages, passing frozen representations forward without joint optimization.
The second stage computes the absolute reconstruction error and trains a backend classifier to predict whether the image is real or generated.
Crucially, this existing architecture lacks direct interaction between the diffusion model and the downstream classifier.
In contrast, the proposed framework unifies reconstruction and classification into an end-to-end training pipeline.
The Frequency Mask Refinement module filters out difficult-to-reconstruct mid-band frequencies to produce a pseudo-generated image.
Both the original and pseudo-generated images are passed to the diffusion autoencoder for parallel reconstruction.
Absolute difference operations calculate distinct reconstruction error maps for both the original and pseudo-generated inputs.
These dual reconstruction error maps are concatenated and fed into the classifier to make the final real or generated prediction.
This integrated design ensures better alignment between artifact generation and artifact detection across the latent space.
The training pipeline begins with three inputs: the input medical image, its corresponding ground truth mask, and generated interactive masks.
A frozen image encoder extracts visual tokens from the input image, while initial interaction simulators derive point, bounding box, and text prompts from the masks.
The system then enters an iterative interaction loop that simulates multiple consecutive refinement steps.
The initial simulated interaction prompts are processed by a learnable prompt encoder.
The extracted image tokens are combined with convolutional feedback features via element-wise addition.
A learnable mask decoder integrates these fused image features with the encoded prompts and circulates intermediate features back through a convolution layer.
Transposed convolution layers then upsample the decoded representations into predicted segmentation masks for both the ground truth and interactive targets.
The framework computes error regions by identifying discrepancies between each predicted mask and its target.
Interaction simulators place corrective prompts on these error regions and feed them back to the prompt encoder, completing the feedback loop across iterations.
The framework begins with a set of unstructured facial images depicting an individual across diverse poses, expressions, and lighting conditions.
These images are processed by the Omni-ID Encoder to construct a comprehensive identity representation.
Each input face is first passed through a shared feature extractor to compute individual token features.
The individual image tokens are concatenated along the token axis into a unified image-set feature representation.
In parallel, a sequence of learnable, semantic-aware query tokens is initialized.
Within the cross-attention layers, the learnable queries attend to the image-set features injected as keys and values to aggregate shared identity attributes.
Subsequent self-attention layers further refine these feature interactions across the token sequence.
Finally, the architecture outputs the holistic Omni-ID embedding, tailored for downstream generative face synthesis.
The uncertainty-aware attention module takes map queries as input, splitting them into two parallel processing branches.
In the upper branch, the queries predict spatial coordinate offsets to be added to reference points.
The summed positions define sampling locations across the bird's-eye-view grid.
Features are sampled directly from the bird's-eye-view feature map at these locations.
This extracts a focused set of sampled spatial features.
Simultaneously, the lower branch feeds the map queries into a multilayer perceptron.
The network outputs mean and variance parameters for dynamic resampling from a Gaussian distribution.
Learned attention weights are formed by incorporating stochastic disturbance into the distribution parameters.
The sampled features and dynamic attention weights are aggregated and projected through a linear layer.
The resulting update terms refine the map queries for generalizable vectorization.
The pipeline begins in the first section with multiple camera views and their corresponding foreground object masks.
These inputs are used to construct an initial set of three-dimensional Gaussians containing the statue.
Depth maps are then rendered across the set of camera viewpoints.
Entering the depth-guided mask inference stage, reference and secondary views are paired with their respective masks.
Applying these masks isolates the visible background regions for both viewpoints.
Using depth from the second view, background content is projected onto the reference view.
This determines the final depth-guided inpainting mask for the reference view.
The mask is transferred into the final inpainting-guided refinement stage.
Inpainting is performed on the reference view to synthesize missing background color and depth.
Depth-guided projection then lifts the inpainted reference view into a three-dimensional surface structure.
This structure initializes the refined Gaussians while projecting background information onto the remaining viewpoints.
Finally, render loss on the reference view and cross-view loss on other rendered views supervise the refined scene.
The tracking framework begins by receiving historical bounding boxes along with consecutive template and search point clouds.
In Stage One, the sequence of past bounding boxes is converted into a history motion vector representing prior trajectories.
This history vector is processed by a box motion encoder to capture global temporal patterns and suppress noise.
The box motion decoder then predicts the subsequent movement using learned temporal tokens.
This yields a coarse estimate of the current motion vector for the target center.
In Stage Two, weight-shared three-dimensional sparse convolution backbones extract geometric features from the template and search point clouds.
Voxel features are transformed into bird's-eye-view representations and processed through top-down feature interaction to learn multi-scale spatial relations.
A bottom-up interaction stream then aggregates and re-weights these multi-scale features using deformable attention.
This produces refined motion-aware feature maps for both the search and template regions.
In the iterative refinement module, the coarse motion vector initializes a motion map while motion-aware features undergo feature matching.
A correlation volume is generated to iteratively sample geometric correspondences and refine the planar motion map.
Concurrently, the regression head predicts the vertical position and heading angle from the search features.
Finally, combining the refined horizontal offsets with the vertical coordinate and orientation outputs the predicted current three-dimensional bounding box.
During training and fine-tuning, the framework learns subject-specific representations without requiring explicit regularization.
An augmented reference image and the current noisy latent are provided as inputs to the Prompt Net.
Prompt Net maps the visual features into a customized concept word embedding.
Inside the Stable Diffusion backbone, the text encoder converts this embedding into conditioning representations.
The UNet network combines the text conditioning with the noisy latent to predict the diffusion noise.
This optimization produces the denoised intermediate state at the current timestep.
During inference, a single user input image and the current noisy sample enter the pipeline.
Prompt Net directly extracts the subject concept embedding representing the target identity.
Fusion Sampling jointly integrates the subject token with arbitrary text prompts, such as in Anime style.
The sampling process yields a stylized generation that fully preserves fine-grained subject details.
Training begins with the Emotion Variation pipeline, which modifies facial expressions based on targeted emotional parameters.
Target emotions are sampled from the continuous valence and arousal space, specifying both emotional polarity and intensity.
An upsampling module projects these continuous valence and arousal values into a higher-dimensional emotion embedding.
Concurrently, the input face image is mapped into the latent space using an inversion module to extract its original latent code.
The latent code and emotion embedding are concatenated and fed into the EmoExtract module to predict an emotion modification direction.
This predicted displacement is added to the original latent code, forming the edited latent representation.
The pretrained generator synthesizes the final image, displaying the desired facial expression.
Pretrained feature encoders compute emotion, pose, background, and identity losses to supervise the variation training.
The pipeline alternates with the Emotion Reconstruction branch to ensure faithful feature disentanglement.
Here, the input face is inverted to its latent code, while an emotion estimator predicts its inherent valence and arousal.
These predicted values are upsampled into the corresponding emotion embedding.
EmoExtract processes the concatenated codes, trained to output a zero vector since no emotional change is needed.
The displacement is added back to the latent code, preserving the original latent representation.
The generator reconstructs the face, maintaining the exact input expression and identity.
Reconstruction, emotion, pose, and identity losses supervise this branch to guarantee high-fidelity image reconstruction.
The pipeline begins with the iterative latent diffusion separation stage to isolate transmission and reflection features.
The input consists of a potentially misaligned flash and no-flash image pair.
Both images are processed through an encoder, reducing spatial dimensions to alleviate registration errors.
This yields a pair of condensed no-flash and flash feature latents.
The latent pair is concatenated and merged with random Gaussian noise.
These noisy concatenated tensors are prepared as input for the denoising network.
A dual-branch UNet performs iterative denoising, leveraging inter-branch cross-attention for joint guidance.
The separation yields two distinct representations: a reflection latent and a transmission latent.
The framework then transitions to the cross-latent decoding stage to reconstruct high-resolution details.
The original captured image is fed into an encoder to provide sharp, unseparated structural cues.
The separated transmission latent enters the decoder directly, receiving fine details through zero-convolution skip connections.
This produces the final, faithfully restored transmission image.
The image encoder begins hierarchical feature extraction, capturing early low-level details at block one.
Block two continues extracting intermediate visual characteristics.
Block three builds deeper contextual representations.
Finally, block four produces high-level abstract semantic features.
The multi-level adapter fusion module processes these multi-tier representations to enhance feature diversity.
The extracted features from each block feed into dedicated learnable adapters.
Each adapter transforms its respective level into an adapted feature representation.
A fusion block then uniformly integrates these adapted representations across all levels.
This produces a unified intermediate fused feature.
Next, the fused feature passes through a frozen projector module.
This yields the final enhanced visual feature, combining fine-grained details with rich semantic information.
The overall architecture begins with the initial compressive sensing measurement data.
A leading residual block transforms the measurements into the intermediate domain of the diffusion model.
This initializes both a three-channel image estimate and a multi-channel feature representation.
The state passes into unfolded Diffusion Message Passing steps, iteratively updating the reconstruction.
The iterations continue down the reverse diffusion trajectory through successive unfolded stages.
The final DMP step completes the message passing sequence.
This yields the fully denoised three-channel image alongside the final feature maps.
A tail residual block converts the output back into the single-channel reconstructed image.
Examining an individual DMP step reveals how each iteration processes its image and feature inputs.
A gradient descent block enforces measurement consistency with a learnable step size.
The gradient-updated state is concatenated with the feature map and processed by a residual block to approximate filtering and divergence terms.
Channel-wise splitting separates the guided diffusion input from the next iteration's feature map.
The pre-trained diffusion model acts as a denoiser, outputting the refined image for the next step.
Each residual block contains an input convolution, four cascaded residual units, and an output convolution.
Within each residual unit, two convolutions with non-linear activation are combined with a skip connection.
The pipeline begins with an input RGB image containing tabletop objects.
An off-the-shelf instance segmentation module detects class labels, bounding boxes, and object masks.
The detected bounding box isolates the specific target object in the scene.
The cropped image patch is then fed simultaneously into two parallel estimation branches.
The Metric Scale Object Shape branch estimates the 3D metric geometry in camera coordinates.
This generates a metric scale mesh aligned with the camera coordinate system.
The predicted metric mesh is then projected onto the image plane via depth rendering.
This produces a dense rendered depth map of the target object.
In parallel, the Normalized Object Coordinate Space branch processes the image patch.
It predicts a canonical coordinate map defined directly in the object reference frame.
A similarity transformation aligns the rendered depth map with the predicted normalized coordinate map.
The final output accurately determines the six-dimensional object pose and bounding box size.
The pipeline begins with the deepfake impersonation attack framework.
The attack leverages diverse datasets encompassing facial replacement, reenactment, and synthesis.
Deepfake video sequences are supplied from these datasets.
An MTCNN model is applied to detect and crop face images from each video frame.
The attacker prepares these cropped celebrity face images for transmission.
Attacks are categorized into targeted impersonation against a specific victim and non-targeted impersonation across any celebrity class.
The attack queries are dispatched to commercial celebrity recognition web APIs.
Evaluation targets black-box platforms including Amazon Rekognition, Azure Cognitive Services, and Naver CFR.
The evaluation module systematically analyzes the resulting responses.

The pipeline begins with a natural language description specifying the desired app layout and behavior.
During preprocessing, the text is tokenized and literal strings are separated into placeholder variables.
The preprocessed sequence is fed into the encoder of a sequence-to-sequence neural network.
The decoder processes the encoded representations to generate target application tokens.
This produces the Simplified App Representation, a compact formal language capturing components and logic.
The dedicated compiler parses the representation to match components with predefined source templates.
It reintroduces the literal strings to output MIT App Inventor source files.
These source files are then passed to the MIT App Inventor backend compiler.
The backend builds the project into a functional Android package ready for deployment.
The pipeline begins by taking raw video frames as visual input.
A visual feature extractor processes the frames to capture scene characteristics.
The video embedder then projects these features into a sequence of video tokens.
Simultaneously, the source subtitle text enters the linguistic pathway.
A text embedder converts the sentence into corresponding text tokens.
The video and text tokens are concatenated to form a unified multimodal sequence.
A cross-modal encoder models contextual interactions between visual and textual features.
The decoder attends to these cross-modal representations to generate translated subtitles.
Translation generation is directly supervised with standard cross-entropy loss.
In parallel, average pooling aggregates the token sequences for contrastive learning.
Dedicated multilayer perceptrons project the pooled modalities into a joint representation space.
This produces matched representation pairs across the visual and textual domains.
A contrastive loss is applied to align shared cross-modal semantics.
The contrastive objective pulls matching positive pairs together while pushing negative pairs apart.
Pairs of experience observations are sampled from the replay buffer.
Each sampled instance pairs raw observation frames with corresponding context parameters across different environment shifts.
The encoders map these contextual observations into a shared latent representation space.
Conditioned on the policy's actions, probabilistic transition models predict the next-state distributions.
Concurrently, reward models estimate expected scalar rewards for each latent state.
Finally, bisimulation losses align latent representation distances with the combined reward differences and Wasserstein transition distances.
The input consists of noisy, mosaicked linear raw images captured directly by the camera sensor.
In the standard workflow, these raw images first undergo traditional postprocessing to generate low dynamic range color images.
This defines the conventional Neural Radiance Field pipeline, which operates on postprocessed low dynamic range inputs.
The standard NeRF model optimizes a volumetric scene representation using rays cast through the processed image views.
Novel low dynamic range views can then be rendered by changing the camera viewpoint, though tone and dynamic range remain fixed.
In contrast, the RawNeRF pipeline bypasses early processing and feeds the raw linear sensor data directly into training.
RawNeRF trains the neural radiance field directly in linear high dynamic range space, learning to denoise the scene jointly.
This allows the pipeline to render full high dynamic range views while simultaneously enabling viewpoint and focus changes.
Finally, postprocessing operations such as exposure control and tonemapping are applied downstream with full HDR flexibility.
The pipeline begins with the synthetic dataset preparation stage.
Fractal system parameters are sampled to construct diverse mathematical configurations.
These sampled parameters are grouped together to define distinct synthetic classes for training.
During pre-training, an image generator renders fractal images on the fly from these parameter codes.
Generated batches of fractal patterns are fed directly into the vision model.
The neural network backbone processes the batch to produce category predictions.
A loss function evaluates the predictions against the synthetic target labels.
Gradients are backpropagated to update the backbone weights throughout pre-training.
For downstream evaluation, real-world image recognition datasets are introduced.
The pre-trained model is fine-tuned to achieve competitive performance across these real-world tasks.

The Florence caption generator extracts descriptive text from each patch.

A pretrained text encoder embeds the caption to provide semantic conditioning.
In parallel, a pretrained image encoder maps the high-resolution patch into latent space.
Gaussian noise is introduced during the forward diffusion process.
This creates the noised latent representation.
A diffusion U-Net is trained from scratch on 38,000 images conditioned on the text embeddings.
The network outputs the predicted noise to optimize diffusion training.
Panel B presents the proposed feature-to-image foundation model training framework.
The same high-resolution smartphone dataset provides the input patches.
A pretrained DINOv2 vision transformer extracts dense visual representations on the fly.
These low-level DINOv2 features provide rich, hallucination-resistant spatial conditioning.
The image is encoded into latent space by the pretrained encoder.
Gaussian noise is added to the latent representation.
This yields the noised latent vector.

It predicts the added noise, learning fine structural priors.
Panel C shows single-image super-resolution adaptation using the text-to-image foundation model.

The RAM captioning module generates descriptive text tags for the image.
The text encoder converts the caption into conditioning vectors.
The image encoder maps the low-resolution input into latent space.

The resulting latent feature is passed to the diffusion backbone.
The previously trained diffusion U-Net is frozen.
LoRA layers adapt the U-Net for single-step restoration.

The pretrained decoder maps the latent feature back to pixel space.

The latent representation is fed to the diffusion backbone.

The pipeline begins with an input image.
The image is first partitioned into a sequence of regular visual patches.
These patches are passed into the hybrid encoder network.
A convolutional encoder extracts low-level local features.
A dedicated class token is prepended alongside spatial position encodings.
This forms the initial full-length sequence of continuous tokens.
Self-attention layers with token merging progressively compress similar tokens.
The global alignment module enriches the learned representations.
The class token is extracted from the encoder output.
It is projected through a multi-layer perceptron head.
And aligned with target representations from a teacher model or ground truth labels.
In parallel, the compressed visual tokens enter the token quantization module.
Positional indices of the merged tokens are retained.
The continuous embedding representations are extracted.
Vector quantization discretizes each token into discrete codes.
This yields a compact set of quantized semantic tokens.
During the generative stage, these discrete tokens drive image generation.
An autoregressive generation process starts with a start token.
The causal decoder synthesizes tokens sequentially with key-value cache compression.
Predicting the compact sequence of quantized tokens.
Next, the source recovery module reconstructs full spatial context.
The quantized tokens are supplied to the recovery cross-attention mechanism.
A set of learnable recovery queries corresponds to all original spatial positions.
Cross-attention models the relationships between original positions and merged tokens.
This predicts the source matrix to establish token assignments.
The token unmerge operation uses these assignments to uncompress the tokens.
Restoring the full sequence length while preserving spatial fidelity.
The restored sequence is then processed by the decoder.
Attention layers perform token dequantization and feature refinement.
Producing dense continuous feature representations.
A convolutional decoder maps features back to image space.
Finally, all patches are reconstructed, generating the final high-resolution image.
The ResCLIP pipeline integrates two core modules to achieve training-free dense vision-language inference.
It builds upon the foundational vision-language architecture of CLIP.
An input image is partitioned into patches and fed to the visual pipeline.
Concurrently, text queries corresponding to target semantic categories are supplied.
The CLIP Visual Encoder extracts visual feature representations across multi-head self-attention layers.
The CLIP Text Encoder computes text embeddings to align with visual tokens.
The Residual Cross-correlation Self-attention module extracts attention across intermediate encoder layers.
In parallel, the Semantic Feedback Refinement module refines attention based on category regions.
Both attention components are fused to remodel the attention in the final layer.
Cosine similarity measures the alignment between dense visual tokens and text representations.
An initial segmentation mask is derived and fed back to guide the semantic refinement module.
After iterative refinement, the system generates the final dense semantic segmentation predictions.
Looking into the Residual Cross-correlation Self-attention module in detail,
visual tokens pass through successive transformer layers.
Cross-correlation self-attention is computed at early intermediate layers,
as well as mid-level layers,
and deeper non-final layers, capturing rich spatial and cross-feature correspondence.
The final block utilizes self-correlation self-attention to preserve spatial covariance.
The cross-correlation attention maps from these non-last layers are averaged,
forming a clear, localized spatial activation map.
This aggregated attention matrix is output as the RCS attention representation.
Next, the Semantic Feedback Refinement module optimizes the attention using category masks.
It takes the initial continuous segmentation map,
and converts it into patch-level category assignments.
An indicator function constructs a binary semantic co-occurrence matrix.
For any given patch, matching categories across the image are highlighted.
A spatial distance-based decay function is applied to prioritize connected local regions,
reducing the influence of disjoint regions of the same class.
A Gaussian smoothing kernel is then applied across the rows,
yielding a smoothly distributed attention map for each patch.
This yields the final refined SFR attention scores.
Finally, the fusion stage combines the attention components.
The RCS attention weights provide cross-feature spatial context.
The SFR attention scores reinforce local semantic consistency.
The noisy, diffuse attention of standard CLIP,
is transformed through weighted attention fusion,
producing a sharp, object-centric attention map for accurate training-free dense inference.
The initializing process begins with a pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splatting model with frozen parameters.
The model is passed into the Frequency Guided Densification module.
Frequency Guided Densification is structured into two main phases shown below.
In Phase 1, the contribution of each 3D Gaussian to rendering quality is evaluated.
Low-contribution 3D Gaussians are removed.
In Phase 2, views are rendered from multiple perspectives.
Each rendered image is split into a grid of patches.
A Discrete Fourier Transform is applied to the patches.
This converts the image patches into transformed frequency representations.
Transformed patches enter the high frequency detection stage.
Each transformed patch is combined via Hadamard product with a quadratic mask.
The quadratic mask highlights high frequency regions.
Patches exhibiting high frequency components are selected.
The 3D Gaussians within these high frequency areas are split into denser elements.
This yields the updated 3D Gaussian Splatting representation after densification.
A gradient mask is constructed across the Gaussian parameter set.
In the fine-tuning process, parameters are unfrozen for model optimization.
Rendering is performed using the fine-tuned 3D Gaussians.
A Discrete Wavelet Transform decomposes the rendered image into frequency sub-bands.
The low frequency component is routed forward.
A pre-trained decoder with frozen parameters processes the low frequency signal.
The decoder outputs the recovered decoded message.
Meanwhile, the high frequency components from the rendered image are extracted.
The ground truth image is introduced for supervision.
A Discrete Wavelet Transform is applied to the ground truth image.
This isolates the high frequency components of the ground truth.
Reconstruction and perceptual loss functions compare rendered views with ground truth.
A wavelet loss is computed between rendered and ground truth high frequencies.
A fixed message serves as target supervision.
Message loss compares the decoded message with the fixed message.
All objectives combine into a single total loss function.
The total loss guides the optimizer.
Finally, the optimizer applies the gradient mask via Hadamard product to update the fine-tuned 3D Gaussians.
The pipeline begins with the multi-resolution feature grid module.
A 3D indoor scene is modeled compositionally from multi-view inputs.
A camera casts viewing rays into the 3D space.
Along each ray, multiple 3D spatial points are sampled.
For each queried point coordinate,
features are queried across multiple grid resolutions, from coarse levels,
down to finer levels using spatial hash tables.
These interpolated features are concatenated and fed into a lightweight neural network.
The network outputs a vector containing signed distance function values for each individual object.
These encompass specific instance geometries, such as pillows,
lamps,
and other segmented items in the scene.
A minimum operation is applied across all object distance predictions,
extracting the global scene signed distance value,
denoted as the overall scene SDF.
Next, the occlusion-aware object opacity module calculates individual object opacities.
Object SDFs are first converted into individual object density distributions.
Concurrently, the global scene transmittance is computed along the ray,
and multiplied by each object's density.
This produces occlusion-aware object opacities that account for frontal blocking.
The composite weight function governs the overall volume rendering contribution.
An object opacity loss is evaluated,
supervising the rendered object opacities directly against 2D instance segmentation masks.
Finally, several regularization and multi-modal rendering losses are optimized.
An Eikonal loss enforces valid distance field gradients across the scene.
An object distinction regularization loss prevents internal collision and overlap between separate instances.
Volume rendering synthesizes geometric cues and appearance.
A scale-invariant depth loss,
supervises rendered depth maps.
A surface normal loss,
aligns predicted surface normals with pseudo-ground-truth,
derived from a pre-trained monocular estimation network.
Lastly, an RGB reconstruction loss,
ensures photorealistic rendering against ground truth captured images.

Given an input crowd image, the Point Query Transformer pipeline begins by extracting visual representations.
A standard CNN backbone processes the input image to extract deep feature representations.
This produces a feature map F, where each spatial element is treated as an individual token.
The feature tokens are passed into a transformer encoder utilizing progressive rectangle-window attention.
Initial encoder layers compute self-attention within large horizontal rectangular windows to capture contextual crowd information.
Subsequent encoder layers progressively reduce the rectangle window size to focus on local regional details efficiently.
The encoder outputs context-enriched image feature representations for the decoding stage.
In parallel, a uniform grid of sparse querying points is initialized across the image canvas.
A region-based quadtree splitter evaluates local image features to determine whether a region is dense or sparse.
Points in dense regions are dynamically split into four sub-points, whereas points in sparse regions remain undivided.
This adaptive quadtree splitting generates denser point queries precisely where high crowd congestion occurs.
The resulting candidate points are paired with sampled CNN features and positional embeddings to form point queries.
In the object querying stage, the transformer decoder decodes sparse queries inside local rectangular windows.
Dense queries are progressively decoded in smaller local windows, modeling relationships guided by image context.
The decoded point queries gather both semantic crowd context and spatial localization information.
These decoded queries are passed in parallel into the multi-layer perceptron prediction head.
For each query, the head predicts a person classification probability along with precise coordinate offsets.
Surplus split queries that land on background regions are classified as containing no person.
Likewise, sparse queries covering empty areas correctly output no-person predictions.
Queries in dense regions successfully detect individual heads with high probability and localized offsets.
The individual point predictions are collected and mapped back onto the original image space.
This yields the final crowd count and precise instance-level localizations across both sparse and congested scenes.

This aggregates the node representations into a unified graph-level embedding vector.
Finally, the embedding is passed to a classification layer that outputs the predicted emotion probabilities.

The pipeline begins with social media posts containing images and captions.
During post collection, relevant public posts are scraped, filtering out invalid entries with a minimal loss.
The collected images and associated metadata are stored in the base repository.
The stored data then proceeds to the preprocessing stage.
Audio description processing cleans the captions to isolate high-quality descriptive text.
Visual features are then extracted from the remaining valid images.

Next, the pipeline transitions to the data analysis stage.
Image clustering organizes visual samples into coherent semantic groups.

At the edge, a connected camera continuously captures raw real-time video frames.
The incoming video stream is simultaneously routed to local inference and an adaptive sampling buffer.
A lightweight student model executes real-time inference directly on the edge to deliver immediate results.
Meanwhile, the adaptive frame sampling module collects and buffers selected video frames for offloading.
These buffered frame batches are compressed and uploaded over the network to the cloud.
In the cloud, an accurate teacher model processes the frames and measures scene change across inputs.
The sampling rate controller dynamically adjusts sampling frequency based on scene variation and edge resource usage.
Concurrently, the online labeling process utilizes teacher model predictions to generate accurate training labels.
The cloud returns the generated labels and sampling rate parameters to the edge device.
The edge device performs adaptive online training with small batches to continually fine-tune the student model.
A replay memory caches intermediate activation volumes during retraining, preventing catastrophic forgetting.
The restoration pipeline begins with a degraded under-display camera face image suffering from blur, low light, and diffraction.
A shallow feature extractor uses a three-by-three convolution to project the image into initial shallow feature maps.
These features are forwarded to the UDC Restoration Module for coarse-grained degradation removal.
The module processes the representations across four consecutive transformer blocks,
effectively capturing global context and local details to clean basic artifacts.
Next, the Dictionary-Guided Restoration Module performs fine-grained facial detail restoration using a symmetric encoder-decoder hierarchy.
In the encoder, the first Dictionary-Guided Transformer Block downsamples spatial resolution while doubling channels.
A second block continues multi-scale feature abstraction to prepare for component-level priors.
At the bottleneck, the model integrates facial component dictionaries.
Dictionary-Guided Multi-head Attention queries high-quality texture priors for eyes, nose, and mouth.
A Gated Feed Forward Network modulates the aggregated facial representations.
Subsequent transformer blocks refine bottleneck features without repeatedly querying the dictionary.
During decoding, bottleneck features concatenate with encoder skip connections.
A decoder transformer block reconstructs higher-resolution spatial details.
Another skip connection fuses earlier multi-scale features,
followed by the final decoder block.
A long skip connection combines initial coarse features with deep restored features.
The Image Reconstruction Module receives the deep features for final image synthesis.
It processes them through four standard transformer blocks,
and applies a final three-by-three convolution,
producing a clear, high-fidelity face image.
Looking closer at the base Transformer Block design:
The input passes through batch normalization.
Pixel-wise and depth-wise convolutions generate queries,
which are reshaped into attention tokens.
Parallel convolutions produce keys,
which are reshaped accordingly.
Similarly, the value projections are generated,
and reshaped.
The queries and keys are multiplied via dot product,
normalized by Softmax across channels,
and applied to the values.
After reshaping back to spatial dimensions,
a pixel-wise convolution projects the attention output,
which is added to the shortcut connection.
The result is processed by the Gated Feed Forward Network.
Inside the Gated Feed Forward Network:
Batch normalization normalizes incoming activations into two parallel paths.
The upper path uses a pixel-wise convolution
followed by Sigmoid activation to create a gating mask.
The lower branch applies pixel-wise and depth-wise convolutions to strengthen locality.
Both paths are element-wise multiplied to gate the feature flow,
and added back to the residual input for the final output.
During the inference phase, the framework inspects an input test image across multiple patch scales.
First, large sixty-four by sixty-four patches are extracted across the image.
Each sixty-four patch is passed through the sixty-four scale encoder.
The encoder outputs the corresponding patch feature embeddings.
These embeddings are matched against the reference normal feature embeddings from training.
The model computes the L2 distance between the extracted features and normal embeddings.
This distance metric forms an initial anomaly map at the sixty-four scale.
A distributed anomaly map is then generated to smooth and interpolate the score distribution.
In parallel, medium thirty-two by thirty-two patches are sampled.
They are processed through the thirty-two scale encoder.
Extracting representative feature vectors for the medium scale.
The reference normal embeddings for scale thirty-two are retrieved.
The L2 distance measures deviation from normal patterns.
Producing the intermediate thirty-two anomaly map.
Which is converted into a distributed anomaly map for the thirty-two resolution.
For fine local details, sixteen by sixteen patches are sampled.
The sixteen scale encoder processes these fine-grained patches.
Generating high-resolution feature embeddings.
These are paired with the normal feature embeddings learned at scale sixteen.
Evaluating the L2 distance at the finest scale.
Constructing the sixteen scale anomaly map.
And producing the corresponding distributed anomaly map.
Finally, the distributed maps across all three scales are combined through element-wise fusion.
Yielding the final anomaly segmentation map that accurately localizes defects.
Training begins with the original multimodal input, comprising the input image, the question, and the ground-truth answer.
A threshold condition governed by a hyperparameter determines whether to synthesize a visual or textual counterfactual.
Along the visual branch, critical image regions are masked to generate a counterfactual image paired with the original question.
Alternatively, along the question branch, key tokens in the question are masked while preserving the original image.
In parallel, the ground-truth answer is routed to the Negative Answer Assignment module.
This module synthesizes a negative answer assignment based on frequency distributions.
The visual question answering model then processes both the original and synthesized counterfactual inputs.
Finally, the overall training loss is computed across both factual and counterfactual pairs to optimize debiased learning.
